summary: This standards-track document defines the Security Event Token, a data structure for statements of fact from an issuer about a subject. These represent security events, such as the issuance or revocation of a credential. A SET is based on the JSON Web Token.

plainLanguage.summary: A small signed note that says something just happened, such as 'this key was cancelled.'

subtitle: A signed JSON Web Token that reports a fact about a security subject, such as a revoked token or a logged-out session.

tldr.problem: Identity and security systems need a common, self-contained way to tell each other that something happened to a subject, such as a token revocation or an account change.
tldr.mechanism: A SET is a JSON Web Token whose claims carry an issuer, a unique ID and an issue time, plus an events claim that maps event-identifier URIs to JSON payloads. It can be signed with JWS and encrypted with JWE.
tldr.outcome: SETs give profiling specifications a shared base format for security events. They state facts, not commands, and the RFC leaves delivery to other documents.

today: RFC 8417 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the base definition of the SET format.

sections.title: Events as Statements of Fact
sections.content:
RFC 8417 defines the Security Event Token (SET), an extensible data structure built on the JSON Web Token (JWT) format. Because it is a JWT, it can optionally be signed with JSON Web Signature (JWS) and encrypted with JSON Web Encryption (JWE), and it can be exchanged over protocols such as HTTP.

A SET describes a statement of fact from the point of view of an issuer about a subject. The subject might be a web resource, a token, an IP address or the issuer itself. Examples the RFC lists include the creation, modification or removal of a resource, the suspension of an account, the revocation of a token before it expires, and the logout of a user session.

The RFC is clear that security events are not commands between parties. A recipient validates and interprets the SET and then takes its own independent action, if any. It may also have no relationship with the subject and do nothing. The specification covers security- and identity-related events, and it defines only a base format. Separate profiling specifications define the actual events.
sections.plainLanguage: A SET is like a news bulletin, not an order. It says what happened, and each reader decides for itself whether to do something about it.

sections.title: Anatomy of a SET
sections.content:
The claims at the top level of the JWT Claims Set are called the envelope. The key one is the events claim, a JSON object that MUST contain at least one member. Each member name is an event identifier, which MUST be a URI. Each member value is the event payload, which MUST be a JSON object holding the claims for that event. An event with no payload claims is written as the empty object {}.

When one SET contains several event identifiers, they are several aspects of the same state transition. They are not a way to bundle distinct events about the same subject. Identifiers with the same value MUST NOT be repeated, and events MUST NOT express multiple independent logical events. Event identifiers SHOULD be stable, such as a permanent URL for an event specification.

The RFC includes non-normative examples: a SCIM password reset, an OpenID back-channel logout, a medical consent notice and an OpenID RISC account-disabled event. In the consent example the payload has its own iss, which names the issuer of the subject. It is distinct from the top-level iss, which is always the issuer of the event.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of an envelope with a label on the outside and a note inside. The label says who sent it, and the note says what happened and to whom.

sections.title: The Core Claims
sections.content:
A SET reuses several registered JWT claims and adds three of its own.

  • iss: the issuer. REQUIRED. The SET issuer need not be the issuer associated with the subject unless a profile says so.
  • iat: when the SET was issued. REQUIRED.
  • jti: a unique identifier, which MUST be unique within an event feed. REQUIRED. Recipients MAY use it to track which SETs they have already received.
  • aud: one or more audiences. RECOMMENDED.
  • sub: the principal the SET is about, usually the entity whose state changed. OPTIONAL. If used, the profile MUST define its content and format.
  • exp: NOT RECOMMENDED, because a SET records something that has already happened.

The new claims are events (described above), txn and toe. The txn claim is an OPTIONAL transaction identifier used to correlate related JWTs. The toe (time of event) claim is an OPTIONAL NumericDate. Leaving it out means the issuer is not sharing an event time.
sections.plainLanguage: Every SET has a few required stickers: who made it, when, and a serial number. A few extra stickers, like which event it is about, are optional.

sections.title: Typing, Signing and Encoding
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type application/secevent+jwt. A SET MAY put it in the JWT typ header parameter to declare that the JWT is a SET, and it MUST do so if the SET could be confused with another kind of JWT in its application context. Following RFC 7515, the application/ prefix is omitted, so the typ value SHOULD be secevent+jwt.

Section 2.4 walks through building a SET. The claims are encoded as in RFC 7519, and the header and claims are base64url-encoded and joined with periods. For simplicity, the worked example is an unsecured token with alg set to none and an empty signature. The RFC notes that when a SET is not signed or encrypted, other mechanisms such as TLS MUST provide integrity protection, confidentiality and issuer authenticity as needed. When auditing or extra transmission security is required, JWS signing and JWE encryption MAY be used, following Section 7 of RFC 7519.
sections.plainLanguage: You can mark the envelope 'this is a SET' so nobody mistakes it for another kind of note. You can also seal it with a signature or lock it, and the plain version in the example is only for teaching.

sections.title: What SET Profiles Must Define
sections.content:
RFC 8417 is a base. A profiling specification defines particular event types, their claims and their processing rules. Profiles SHOULD define syntax, semantics, subject identification and validation.

  • Syntax: the top-level claims and the event payload format.
  • Semantics: above all, how to validate the issuer and obtain the keys it used. If a profile allows or requires an unsecured JWT, it MUST specify how integrity is ensured.
  • Subject identification: profiles MUST define how the subject is identified, and how to tell the subject's issuer from the SET issuer. Using sub is NOT RECOMMENDED when the subject is not globally unique and has a different issuer.
  • Validation: profiles MUST clearly specify the steps a recipient MUST perform to check that the SET is syntactically and semantically valid.

Profiles also decide how to treat multiple event identifiers. Some might ignore unknown ones, which allows extension. Others might require that all be understood, or allow only a single one.
sections.plainLanguage: The SET rules are the blank form. Each profile fills it in for one purpose and says exactly how to check that it was filled in correctly.

sections.title: Avoiding Confusion with Other Tokens
sections.content:
Because RFC 7519 says claims that are not understood MUST be ignored, a SET could be mistaken for another JWT from the same issuer, or the other way around. Section 4 gives techniques to prevent this.

  • ID Tokens: if a SET could otherwise pass as an ID Token, its profile MUST require that exp is absent. Since exp is required in ID Tokens, they will reject such a SET. Explicit typing does not help here, because ID Token validation does not look at typ.
  • Access tokens: profiles are encouraged to prohibit exp, use a separate aud value, check for an events claim in access token validation, or use explicit typing.
  • Other JWTs: the most direct way is explicit typing. Others are rejecting JWTs that contain events unless they are meant to be SETs, or leaving out claims the target kind requires, such as sip_callid for RFC 8055 or orig for RFC 8225.
sections.plainLanguage: Some notes look alike, so you add a clear mark that makes the wrong reader refuse it. It is like a ticket for one show that a different show's door won't accept.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
SETs may carry sensitive data, so distribution methods SHOULD require transport-layer security. Parties MUST support TLS 1.2 or higher, and a TLS client MUST check the server certificate. SETs sent through third parties or carrying personally identifiable information MUST be encrypted with JWE or protected for confidentiality by other means. Unless integrity is ensured otherwise, a SET MUST be signed with JWS by a trusted issuer.

The RFC defines no delivery mechanism and no way to order SETs. Order may matter, as in provisioning, where an object cannot be changed before it is created, or for login and logout status. Clocks drift in distributed systems, so timestamps such as iat alone do not guarantee order. Timing also matters: a revocation SET that arrives just as a user logs in again could wrongly end the new session.

On privacy, issuers SHOULD tailor SETs to what recipients need, and SHOULD try to avoid propagating subject identifiers, for example by passing a salted hash. Recipients might correlate events using iat or very precise toe values, so issuers SHOULD take steps to limit correlation, such as using approximate toe values or delaying issuance.
sections.plainLanguage: A note about someone can be private, so you put it in a locked box and sign it. Notes may arrive in the wrong order, so a good sender thinks about that.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered three claims in the JSON Web Token Claims registry: events (Security Events), toe (Time of Event) and txn (Transaction Identifier). The change controller is the IESG.

The RFC also registers the +jwt structured syntax suffix, which indicates that a media type is encoded as a JWT, and the application/secevent+jwt media type, which indicates that the content is a SET.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors put the new sticker names and the new envelope label in the official list, so everyone uses them the same way.
